messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Keanu finds it hardest in the late afternoons, when the light begins to fade. As an electrician, this used to be the time of day he’d be packing up his tools, satisfied with a finished job. Now, it’s a countdown. The assault happened at 4:15 PM, and as the clock ticks towards that time, a familiar, dreadful sense of unreality begins to creep in. It starts as a slight buzzing in his ears, a feeling of being behind a pane of glass, watching himself go through the motions. He knows this feeling is a prelude to the memories, and the panic that follows is sharp and absolute. Six months ago, he was on a routine call, rewiring an older home. The client seemed friendly enough until it came time to settle the bill. The disagreement escalated with a speed that still makes no sense to Keanu. He remembers it only in searingly clear, disconnected images, like still photographs from a nightmare. There is the picture of the client’s face, contorted with rage. There is the picture of the heavy front door slamming shut, the sound of the bolt echoing in the small entryway. There is the picture of the floorboards, inches from his face. The rest is a blur, a frustrating void that his mind refuses to fill. He feels like he is only remembering parts of what happened, and this incompleteness feeds a profound sense of guilt. When the snapshots surface, so does the crushing certainty that he is to blame.

This belief—that the assault happened because of the sort of person he is—has become the foundation of his new reality. He is convinced that someone else, someone smarter or stronger, would not have gotten into this situation. They would have seen the warning signs, would have said the right thing, would have found a way out. This internal narrative of personal failure haunts him. At work, the familiar environment has become a minefield. The slam of a door down a hallway can cause him to drop his tools and freeze, his heart hammering against his ribs. He flinches violently if a coworker approaches him from behind, a simple tap on the shoulder feeling like an attack. This hyper-reactivity to unexpected movement or touch has made him isolated on job sites. He has started turning down jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods, telling his boss he’s overbooked, because the thought of walking into a new house, unable to assess the potential danger, is paralyzing. This avoidance is beginning to threaten his livelihood, the one part of his old self he thought he could hold onto.

His home life offers little respite. His partner, Leilani, tries to be patient, but she admits she feels like she’s living with a ghost. Keanu recoils from her unexpected touch, and their physical intimacy has vanished. In the evenings, he retreats not to her, but to the blue light of his phone, losing hours to mindless games and scrolling, anything to keep the snapshots at bay. When that fails, he turns to alcohol, drinking until the sharp edges of his anxiety are dulled into a manageable haze. He can no longer watch the news or action films; any depiction of violence, even fictional, feels too close, too real. He has come to believe he has no future. The man he was—confident, easy-going, skilled—is gone, replaced by this hollowed-out version, and he sees no path back. It was last week, after he recoiled from Leilani’s embrace with a choked cry, that she told him she couldn’t watch him disappear anymore. He is seeking help now not with any real hope, but out of a desperate fear of losing the last person who remembers who he used to be. What frightens him most is the suspicion that he is right, that the event didn’t just happen to him, but revealed him for the failure he has always been.
